title: After a Week of Outages, More Americans Are Stocking Up — Just in Case
summary:
Teri Brown worried about what her family would do if the U.S. electrical grid went down. So she and her husband Richard stocked their Denver home with food and two 55-gallon tanks of extra water.

They are now "preppers" — people who get ready for worst cases. Brown, 47, says the label carries a stigma. Preppers are often shown as extremists stockpiling food.

That image may be changing: Microsoft kept Outlook users from email, Apple Pay stopped working, and last Friday airports faced a nationwide ground stop.

Many now feel unprepared and turn to preppers for tips. Krystal Christensen, with over 400,000 followers, says ten times as many people ask questions. She says buy only what you need and eat, not to panic-buy.

Even so, generators at her Utah Costco were nearly gone, and an emergency radio named by Derrick James sold out in two days on Amazon.

Deanne Criswell, former head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, says prepare for the risks where you live, not panic-buy. Monique Imroth, 64, agrees — her risk is wildfires.
why_it_matters: Knowing what your family would do if the power or water went out helps you feel calmer and ready, just like practicing a fire drill at school.

keywords.explanation: Preppers are people who get ready for worst cases by keeping extra supplies at home.
A stigma is a bad or unfair idea that people have about a person or a group.
Extremists are people with very strong, extreme views or habits that most people do not share.
Stockpiling means storing up large amounts of food or supplies for later.
A generator is a machine that makes electricity when the normal power supply stops working.

background_read: Preppers are people who keep extra food, water, and supplies at home so they are ready if something goes wrong.
They prepare for emergencies such as losing power or water, or a big storm.
After a week of outages that stopped email, payments, and flights, more people began asking preppers for advice on getting ready.

WHAT: More Americans are stocking up on supplies after a week of outages, and turning to preppers for tips.
WHERE: In homes across the United States, including Denver and Utah.
WHY: Recent outages for email, payments, and flights made many people feel unprepared.
